name: Aristobulus
title: Person mentioned in connection with a Christian household in Rome
summary:
Aristobulus is mentioned indirectly in Paul's letter to the Romans, where the apostle sends greetings to those who belong to his household (Romans 16:10).  
Paul does not greet Aristobulus directly, which may suggest that he himself was not a Christian or that he was already dead when the letter was written.  
Several scholars have proposed that he can be identified with Aristobulus of Alexandria, a grandson of Herod the Great who lived in Rome.  
Regardless of his own faith, his household clearly included Christian believers known to the church in Rome.

keyEvents.title: Greeting to Aristobulus' household
keyEvents.description: In his letter to the church in Rome, Paul sends greetings to those who belong to Aristobulus' household. The wording suggests that Aristobulus himself is not greeted directly, but that there were Christians among his household members—possibly slaves, freedmen, or family members.

versions.summary: Aristobulus is briefly mentioned in Paul's letter to the Romans as a person whose household the apostle sends greetings to. He was likely a prominent Christian in Rome, possibly of Jewish or Greek origin, with a household that included believers.
versions.title: Christian in Rome
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Christian in Rome' is somewhat imprecise. Aristobulus is mentioned only indirectly through his household, and it is unclear whether he himself was a Christian. A more accurate title would reflect this.; [major] The role 'leader' lacks biblical support. Paul greets only those who belong to the household of Aristobulus (Romans 16:10), not Aristobulus himself. There is no indication that he was a leader in the church. He may even have been an unbelieving head of household with Christians in his family.; [major] The summary refers to Aristobulus as 'a prominent Christian in Rome,' but the text in Romans 16:10 greets those 'who belong to the household of Aristobulus' – not Aristobulus himself. This may suggest that Aristobulus was either not a Christian or already deceased. Many scholars identify him with Aristobulus of Alexandria, grandson of Herod the Great, who lived in Rome. The summary should reflect this uncertainty.; [minor] The second key event ('The household as a believing community') is speculative and not directly supported by the text. Verse 11 concerns Herodion, Paul's relative, not specifically the household of Aristobulus. The connection is weak.; [minor] Romans 16:11 refers to Herodion and those belonging to the household of Narcissus, not the household of Aristobulus. Verse 11 should be removed from this reference or the event should be rephrased.; [major] Footnotes providing historical context are missing. Aristobulus is an interesting figure with possible links to the Herodian dynasty, and this should be addressed.

footnotes.text: Several early church historians and scholars have identified this Aristobulus with Aristobulus of Alexandria, grandson of Herod the Great, who lived in Rome during the reign of Emperor Claudius. If this identification is correct, it explains why Paul greets his household but not him personally—he may have been dead, or he himself was not a Christian.

The Greek expression 'tous ek tōn Aristoboulou' (τοὺς ἐκ τῶν Ἀριστοβούλου) literally means 'those of Aristobulus [household]', that is, members of his household. The wording suggests that Aristobulus himself was not among those greeted, which differs from other greetings in Romans 16 where individuals are greeted directly.

The fact that Paul greets Herodion, whom he calls his kinsman (syngenē), in the following verse (Rom 16:11) has led to speculation about a connection between Aristobulus' household and the Herodian court. The name Herodion may indicate an association with the Herodian dynasty.

In the early church, household fellowships (oikos structures) were central to Christian practice. Slaves and freedmen in a prominent person's household could form their own Christian group, even if the head of the household was not himself a believer.
